# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a potentially life-threatening form of idiopathic systolic heart failure that develops toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause [1]. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group defines PPCM as heart failure secondary to left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction (typically ejection fraction [EF] <45%) occurring in the last month of pregnancy or within five months postpartum [2]. It remains an important contributor to maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide [3].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography, ranging from approximately 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births in the United States, with substantially higher rates reported in Nigeria and Haiti [4,5]. Recognized risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, preeclampsia and other hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and African ancestry [6,7]. Registry data from the EURObservational Research Programme have highlighted significant regional differences in presentation and outcomes [8].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but is increasingly viewed as a "two-hit" model combining systemic angiogenic imbalance with individual susceptibility [9]. A central mechanism involves oxidative stress leading to cleavage of the nursing hormone prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic and proapoptotic fragment, which damages the myocardial microvasculature [10]. Impaired cardiac signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) activity reduces antioxidant defenses, facilitating this cascade [10]. Additionally, soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), secreted by the placenta, exerts antiangiogenic effects that contribute to endothelial and cardiac dysfunction, linking PPCM mechanistically to preeclampsia [11]. A genetic predisposition is supported by the finding that truncating variants in *TTN* (titin) and other cardiomyopathy genes are overrepresented in affected women, suggesting overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy [12,13].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

PPCM commonly presents with dyspnea, orthopnea, peripheral edema, and fatigue—symptoms that may overlap with normal late pregnancy, contributing to delayed diagnosis [14]. Echocardiography is the cornerstone of diagnosis, demonstrating reduced LV systolic function with or without chamber dilation [2]. Natriuretic peptides (BNP/NT-proBNP) are typically elevated and assist in differentiating PPCM from physiological changes [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can aid in tissue characterization and exclusion of alternative etiologies, though gadolinium use is limited during pregnancy [16]. Diagnosis remains one of exclusion, requiring careful evaluation for pre-existing cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, and other causes [1].

## Management

Management of PPCM follows general heart failure principles, modified for pregnancy and lactation [17]. During pregnancy, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are contraindicated, whereas beta-blockers (preferably beta-1 selective) and hydralazine with nitrates may be used safely [18]. After delivery, guideline-directed medical therapy can be fully implemented [17]. Anticoagulation is recommended given the heightened thromboembolic risk associated with both pregnancy and severe LV dysfunction [19].

Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist that blocks prolactin release, has emerged as a disease-specific therapy targeting the prolactin–cathepsin D pathway. The randomized German trial demonstrated improved LV recovery with bromocriptine added to standard therapy, and it must be accompanied by prophylactic anticoagulation [20,21]. The 2019 position statement of the ESC Study Group on PPCM provides a structured "BOARD" approach (Bromocriptine, Oral heart failure therapies, Anticoagulants, vasoRelaxing agents, Diuretics) [22]. For acute decompensation and cardiogenic shock, levosimendan and mechanical circulatory support, including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, may be required [23]. A minority of women with refractory disease progress to cardiac transplantation or durable ventricular assist devices [24].

## Prognosis and Recovery

PPCM carries a more favorable prognosis than other dilated cardiomyopathies, with myocardial recovery (EF >50%) occurring in roughly 50–70% of women, often within six to twelve months [25,26]. However, outcomes vary geographically, and persistent dysfunction, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, and death remain concerns [27]. Lower baseline EF and greater LV dilation at diagnosis predict poorer recovery [26]. The IPAC study provided detailed prospective data on recovery trajectories in a North American cohort [25].

## Subsequent Pregnancy

Subsequent pregnancy poses significant risk, particularly in women with incomplete recovery, in whom relapse, worsening heart failure, and death have been reported [28]. Women who recover normal LV function fare better but still warrant close surveillance [29]. Comprehensive counseling regarding contraception and the risks of future pregnancy is an essential component of care [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is a distinct, partially reversible cardiomyopathy with emerging disease-specific therapies such as bromocriptine. Early recognition, multidisciplinary management, and informed reproductive counseling are crucial to optimizing maternal outcomes. Continued research into its pathophysiology and genetics promises to refine future treatment.
